title: https://www.securityweek.com/meta-says-hackers-took-code-personal-data-of-1500-in-github-breach#DataBreach #GitHub #Meta #CyberSecurity #InfoSec #CodeHeistAlert (3/3)
text:
Meta is notifying roughly 1,500 people, most of them employees in the US, that their personal information was impacted after hackers got into some of the company’s GitHub repositories.

The intrusion was detected a few weeks ago. According to the tech giant, an outside group gained access to the repositories using an employee’s stolen credentials.

Meta’s security team shut down the attackers’ access and brought in GitHub and law enforcement. Notifications to the impacted individuals started going out on Tuesday.

Meta told SecurityWeek that 99% of the data the hackers took was business data, in the form of software code related to some of its products. The remaining 1% was personal data.

That personal data had been added to the repositories by mistake and should not have been there, as storing it on GitHub went against company policy. Meta has not said what types of personal information were involved.

The company also noted that a significant portion of what looked like personal data was actually synthetic or anonymized test data. As a result, the attackers may not readily be able to tell genuine records apart from test data.

Based on its investigation with GitHub so far, Meta does not believe the hackers were specifically after its data.

Meta is also notifying regulators, and the people whose information was involved are being offered credit and dark web monitoring services.

“This was not a vulnerability in any Meta product, and Meta’s internal systems were not breached. Meta business data held in a GitHub repository was improperly accessed using an employee’s stolen credentials – this included a small amount of personal data for a limited number of people, most of whom were Meta employees,” a Meta spokesperson told SecurityWeek.

In response to the incident, Meta rotated secrets it found in the affected repositories. It also hardened its product security to address risks stemming from access to its business data.

The company is working with its teams that use GitHub to keep user data off the platform. As a second line of defense, it is adding controls for proactive scanning to detect any user data uploaded by mistake.

“We’ve since rotated secrets found in the repositories, implemented new controls to prevent user data from being stored in GitHub, and worked with GitHub on additional measures to protect our repositories,” the spokesperson said.

October 13, 2026, marked a busy day for threat intelligence trackers, with numerous data breaches reported across a wide range of industries and geographies. According to breach monitoring service BreachSense, multiple threat actor groups were active, claiming responsibility for attacks on companies in technology, manufacturing, logistics, legal services, and education. The incidents underscore the persistent and global nature of cyber threats, affecting organizations of all sizes and sectors.

Threat Overview
The reported breaches were attributed to several distinct threat actor groups, each targeting different organizations:

OROVA: Claimed a breach against Amantya Technologies, a technology and product engineering company.
n0n: A particularly active group, claimed responsibility for attacks on:
Apical Group (vegetable oil processor, Singapore)
April Group (pulp and paper manufacturer, Indonesia)
Bukit Kayu Hitam ICD (logistics, Malaysia)
Camellia Line (marine transportation, Japan)

Albertin Alcide & Figli

INC_RANSOM: Claimed an attack on Brooks Law Firm in the United States.
Other Victims: Advanced Imaging Solutions (U.S. business technology) was also listed among the victims, with the actor not specified in the summary.

This flurry of activity from different groups simultaneously demonstrates the decentralized and widespread nature of the cybercrime ecosystem.
Technical Analysis
While specific TTPs for each breach were not detailed, the list represents a typical cross-section of cybercriminal activity. The involvement of groups like INC_RANSOM suggests ransomware operations (T1486 - Data Encrypted for Impact) combined with data theft for double extortion. The targeting of manufacturing, logistics, and agribusiness companies highlights the continued focus on sectors that are sensitive to operational disruption. The geographic diversity of the victims (North America, Europe, Asia) confirms that these threat groups operate on a global scale.
Impact Assessment
Each of these breaches carries the potential for significant impact, including financial loss, operational downtime, data loss, and reputational damage. For the manufacturing and logistics companies, a successful ransomware attack can halt production and supply chains. For legal and technology firms, the theft of sensitive client data or intellectual property can be devastating. This summary serves as a stark reminder that no industry is immune and that organizations must maintain a constant state of vigilance.

title: La rente du calcul. L’intelligence artificielle émirienne entre diversification post-pétrole et réalignement stratégique
text:
La rente du calcul. L’intelligence artificielle émirienne entre diversification post-pétrole et réalignement stratégique

Citer

Partager

Imprimeren PDF

Ajouter aux favoris

Léa Samara
Contributrice du Programme Moyen-Orient Afrique du Nord et de l’Observatoire numérique et technologies émergentes de l’IRIS

Depuis trois ans, les Émirats arabes unis occupent le premier rang des récits consacrés à l’essor de l’intelligence artificielle (IA) hors des deux grandes puissances technologiques que sont les États-Unis et la Chine. L’ampleur des sommes engagées, la mise en scène des annonces et la présence répétée d’Abou Dabi aux côtés des géants américains ont installé une lecture désormais convenue, celle d’un pétro-État qui achète, à force d’investissements souverains, son autonomie et sa place dans la révolution algorithmique. Toutefois, cette lecture est incomplète, à deux titres.

Elle confond d’abord des documents d’ordre distinct, souvent invoqués indistinctement. L’Abu Dhabi Economic Vision 2030, adoptée par l’émirat dès 2008, est un plan de diversification économique antérieur au tournant de l’IA. « We the UAE 2031 », vision fédérale lancée en novembre 2022, fixe un cap national général articulé autour de la prospérité, de l’influence et de l’économie de la connaissance. La substance proprement algorithmique se loge, elle, dans la National Strategy for Artificial Intelligence 2031, annoncée en octobre 2017, qui vise à faire des Émirats l’un des leaders mondiaux du secteur et fait de la fédération le premier État au monde à nommer un ministre chargé de l’intelligence artificielle. Cet empilement révèle une continuité ; l’IA y est pensée comme le dernier avatar d’un projet de diversification engagé de longue date.

Deuxièmement, ce que la trajectoire émirienne donne à voir n’est pas une simple diversification, mais la conversion d’une rente pétrolière en une rente du calcul, et cette conversion, présentée comme une conquête de souveraineté, opère en réalité un réalignement stratégique sur l’écosystème américain. La souveraineté algorithmique d’Abou Dabi se paie d’une dépendance négociée et assumée à l’égard des puces, du cloud et des protocoles de sécurité des États-Unis. Le calcul devient, pour l’émirat, ce que le pétrole fut au vingtième siècle, une ressource stratégique dont la maîtrise définit son rang international. Dans quelle mesure la souveraineté que revendique Abou Dabi relève-t-elle d’une émancipation ou d’une dépendance reconfigurée ? Éprouver cette dernière hypothèse suppose d’examiner successivement la logique du pari émirien, l’appareil qui le met en œuvre, puis le prix et la portée géopolitique de ce basculement.

Proche et Moyen-Orient, monde méditerranéen

1 min. de lecture

Pascal Boniface

Directeur de l’IRIS

Sylvie Bermann
Ambassadeur de France en Chine (2011), au Royaume-Uni (2014) et en Russie (2017) et autrice de « Madame l’ambassadeur : de Pékin à Moscou, une vie de diplomate » (Éditions Tallandier, 2022)

La rivalité entre les États-Unis et la Chine a franchi un cap historique lors de la visite d’État de Xi Jinping à Washington à la fin du mois de septembre. Pour la première fois, Washington a semblé se comporter d’égal à égal vis-à-vis de Pékin. Une reconnaissance symbolique qui intervient au moment où les errements de la politique étrangère de Donald Trump, en Iran et en Ukraine, interrogent sur la capacité des États-Unis à tenir tête à la Chine, notamment concernant Taïwan. La multiplication des ingérences de Washington sur l’Amérique latine, où la Chine a grandement développé son influence au cours des dernières années, représente cependant un défi de taille pour cette dernière. L’Europe, peine quant à elle à tirer son épingle du jeu, prise en tenaille entre les deux grandes puissances mondiales.

La Chine ressort-elle vainqueur de la rencontre entre Donald Trump et Xi Jinping ? Comment Taïwan peut-il être impacté par les évolutions de la politique étrangère de Trump ? Pékin a-t-elle un pouvoir d’influence sur la guerre en Iran et en Ukraine ? Enfin, face à ces deux grandes puissances, qu’en est-il de la place de la France et de l’Europe ?

Autant d’enjeux abordés avec Sylvie Bermann, ambassadeur de France en Chine (2011), au Royaume-Uni (2014) et en Russie (2017) et autrice de « Madame l’ambassadeur : de Pékin à Moscou, une vie de diplomate » (Éditions Tallandier, 2022).

title: Trump et Poutine : l’Ukraine en partage
text:
Trump et Poutine : l’Ukraine en partage

3 min. de lecture

Citer

Partager

Imprimeren PDF

Ajouter aux favoris

Romuald Sciora

Chercheur associé à l’IRIS, directeur de l’Observatoire politique et géostratégique des États-Unis

Je n’ai guère été surpris par les déclarations de Donald Trump ces derniers jours sur l’Ukraine. Pas davantage par le deal sur le diesel russe annoncé vendredi, ni par ses appels à remplacer Volodymyr Zelensky. « Je suggère qu’ils se trouvent un nouveau dirigeant capable de négocier », a-t-il lâché samedi. Ni même par sa proclamation dominicale d’un « cessez-le-feu énergétique » dont ni Moscou ni Kiev n’avaient été informés. Zelensky a répondu, sidéré : « Si Trump l’a négocié avec Poutine, qu’il nous dise quand ça commence. » La Russie continuait de frapper les infrastructures énergétiques ukrainiennes quelques heures après l’annonce.

Tout cela était prévisible. Pour plusieurs raisons.

La première : Trump n’a jamais pu sentir Zelensky. Nous avons tous en mémoire la rencontre désastreuse de février 2025 à la Maison-Blanche, ce face-à-face tendu qui avait tourné au pugilat diplomatique sous les caméras. Depuis, quelques inflexions, quelques compliments de façade, « vos soldats sont courageux », « vous avez une belle veste », mais les faveurs du président américain ont toujours été pour Vladimir Poutine.

La deuxième raison est circonstancielle. Donald Trump est à trois semaines des élections de mi-mandat. Sa base MAGA, celle qui l’avait élu en 2024 notamment parce qu’il avait promis de ne pas entraîner l’Amérique dans une nouvelle guerre à l’irakienne ou à l’afghane, ne lui a pas pardonné l’Iran. Les prix à la pompe explosent. En levant les sanctions sur le diesel russe, Trump joue les médecins après avoir lui-même contribué à rendre le patient malade. Bonus : il se trouve désormais un méchant commode. Ce n’est plus à cause de la guerre en Iran si les Américains souffrent à la caisse. C’est à cause de Zelensky, ce président ukrainien obtus qui s’obstine à harceler les raffineries russes au lieu d’accepter la paix que Washington lui tend sur un plateau.

La troisième raison est idéologique. Les connexions entre la Maison-Blanche et le Kremlin ne sont plus un secret pour personne. Elles sont assumées, presque revendiquées. Mais au-delà de ces rapprochements politiques, il existe une véritable communauté de vues. JD Vance, Susie Wiles et les idéologues de l’extrême droite américaine au pouvoir depuis janvier 2025 partagent avec Poutine une même détestation du système multilatéral libéral de l’après-1945, une même fascination pour la loi du plus fort et une même vision du monde où les grandes puissances se partagent des zones d’influence sans se soucier des petits États souverains coincés entre elles.

Et c’est là que se dessinerait la véritable stratégie. Car le Trump d’aujourd’hui n’a plus rien à voir avec celui de 2017, Ubu isolé et improvisateur. Il est désormais entouré d’hommes et de femmes qui savent parfaitement ce qu’ils veulent. Le calcul pourrait être le suivant : resserrer les liens avec Moscou, faire suffisamment de concessions au Kremlin pour qu’il accepte un accord, mais en s’assurant que l’Ukraine résiste encore un minimum, afin que les ambitions de Poutine ne reviennent pas à ce qu’elles étaient en 2022 : l’absorption totale du pays. Zelensky serait poussé vers la sortie. Un président ukrainien plus « accommodant » le remplacerait. Un deal serait signé. Et Donald Trump se présenterait en garant d’une Ukraine libre, du moins de ce qu’il en resterait, en échange d’un accès illimité aux matières premières ukrainiennes. En gros, le même coup qu’avec le Venezuela : une forme de néocolonisation habillée en victoire pour la paix.

Nous assisterions donc à un partage de l’Ukraine. Malgré ce qu’en disent les optimistes qui croient encore à une victoire militaire ukrainienne et se réfugient dans le déni, c’est malheureusement, à mes yeux, le scénario vers lequel nous nous dirigeons. Sept sénateurs […]

title: Le monde au-delà des États, une géopolitique des acteurs non étatiques

Le monde au-delà des États, une géopolitique des acteurs non étatiques

1 min. de lecture

Citer

Partager

Imprimeren PDF

Ajouter aux favoris

Lukas Aubin

Directeur de recherche à l’IRIS, responsable du Programme Sport et géopolitique et de l’Observatoire géopolitique de l’espace post-soviétique

Fatou Élise Ba

Chercheuse à l’IRIS, responsable du Programme Sécurité humaine

Les États souverains dominent nos représentations du monde. Pourtant, une part croissante des fonctions traditionnellement attachées à la souveraineté se déploie hors du seul cadre étatique. Multinationales, plateformes numériques, diasporas, organisations non gouvernementales (ONG), organisations sportives, groupes armés ou entités en quête de reconnaissance investissent des domaines que l’État leur concède, qui échappent à sa maîtrise ou dont le contrôle lui est disputé. Ces formes de pouvoir ne sont pas nouvelles, mais l’échelle de leurs moyens, leur transnationalité et leurs capacités à exercer des formes d’autorité modifient les rapports de force internationaux.

À l’occasion de la parution de la Revue internationale et stratégique (RIS) N°143 sur le thème « Le monde au-delà des États, une géopolitique des acteurs non étatiques », Lukas Aubin, directeur de recherche à l’IRIS, responsable du Programme Sport et géopolitique et de l’Observatoire géopolitique de l’espace post-soviétique, et Fatou Élise Ba, chercheuse à l’IRIS, responsable du Programme Sécurité humaine répondent à nos questions :

Pourquoi est-il devenu indispensable d’analyser les rapports de force entre acteurs non étatiques et puissances étatiques ?

Comment ces pouvoirs alternatifs parviennent-ils à la fois à avoir une capacité d’influence ou de contraindre un État, tout en restant dépendant structurellement de celui-ci ?

Où se situe la frontière juridique et politique entre un État de facto et un État de jure ?

Équilibres internationaux et mondialisation

How Claude Code’s 256KB blind spot put developers’ secrets in the preview pane

News

Oct 14, 20265 mins

Simply asking Anthropic’s Claude Code to review an HTML file could hand attackers access to a developer’s machine, cloud credentials and software development environment, according to a new Noma Security finding.

Noma’s researchers found a vulnerability affecting Anthropic’s Claude Code Desktop app that could allow malicious JavaScript embedded in an HTML file to execute without further user interaction, potentially exposing sensitive host files. The flaw, called SneakPeek, specifically affected the application’s automated preview pane, which renders HTML files generated or modified by Claude.

“This is a strong example of how emerging technologies are reshaping the attack surface,” said Ronald Lewis, head of cybersecurity governance at Black Duck. “Attackers are increasingly targeting the AI ecosystem, exploiting implicit trust relationships between models, agents, tools, data sources, and connected services.”

An attacker could exploit the bug by planting a malicious file in a public repository and waiting for a developer to ask Claude Code to inspect it, Noma said in a blog post shared with CSO ahead of its publication on Wednesday.

Once the application rendered the file, the script could read local files and exfiltrate sensitive data, including AWS credentials, GitHub secrets and SSH private keys, to a remote server.

The flaw has been assigned a high-severity CVSS score of 8.7, while a CVE ID is not yet available. Noma says Anthropic collaborated with Noma Labs during the disclosure process and fully resolved the issue.

“Anthropic confirmed they are preparing a GitHub Security Advisory and have requested a CVE for it,” Eli Ainhorn, senior AI vulnerability researcher at Noma, told CSO. “We expect it to be available soon. The CVSS score is 8.7 High (v4.0), assigned by Anthropic.

Anthropic did not immediately respond to CSO’s request for comment.

A 256KB threshold allowed local files to leak

Noma traced SneakPeek to three architectural gaps in Claude Code Desktop’s preview mechanism, which uses an Electron-based Chromium rendering panel to display HTML content.

The first involved a file-size threshold that changed how the application handled HTML documents. Files smaller than 256KB were converted into base64-encoded data: URLs with a strict Content Security Policy (CSP) that blocked script execution. Files exceeding that threshold were instead written to disk and loaded directly as “file://” URLs, bypassing the CSP protections applied to smaller files.

The second problem was the origin assigned to the rendered content. Loading the larger files through file:// gave the preview renderer access to the local filesystem in Chromium rather than confining it to an isolated, opaque origin, the researchers said.

The third weakness was an inactive request filter. Although the application has a mechanism intended to block file: // access, Noma found that the filter was not active during static file rendering, including when developers reviewed local code test reports.

“Relying on size-based thresholds or client-side filters for security boundaries is inherently fragile,” Lewis said. “Development machines hold high-value operational secrets—SSH private keys, AWS credentials, Kubernetes configurations, and OAuth session tokens.”

Compromising a developer’s local workstation is effectively a direct route into corporate cloud infrastructure, he warned.

Noma found that Anthropic’s initial patch could be bypassed. “The initial patch blocked the preview pane from making direct file read requests from the main page context, but we found that by moving the file-reading code into a Web Worker, a background thread that browsers run separately from the main page, the requests originated from a context the patch didn’t cover,” Ainhorn explained.

The researchers reported the bypass, prompting a […]

The bug was simple: the login let you choose where your sign-in code went. Proving it on a live website was the hard part.

TL;DR

During an authorized assessment, an AI pentesting agent found a critical authentication bypass on a major insurer's production website, on its own.
One login request let the user choose where the one-time passcode went.
The attack was the easy part. Proving it on a live site took web context built over a decade.

The Login Worked. Then the Agent Stopped.

Reflectiz's AI pentesting agent was mapping the login flow of a major insurer's production website, which has millions of users.

The agent requested a login code and directed it to an email inbox it controlled. The code arrived. The login went through. Its guardrails halted the test after the login succeeded.

The agent had discovered a critical-severity authentication bypass on its own. Reflectiz reported it to the insurer.

The Flaw: The Request Chose Where the Code Went

A one-time passcode (OTP) only proves who you are if it goes somewhere already linked to the account. Here, that link was broken.

The login request carried two fields that decided delivery: the channel and the address. Normally, the code went by text to the phone number on the account. But the request could change the channel. Switch it to email, and the server sent the code to whatever address the request named, not the address registered to the account.

Simplified, the request looked like this:

The server never checked that the address belonged to the account.

Binding a code to its account is one of the most basic checks in authentication. OWASP's testing guide asks this in plain words: "Are the OTPs tied to the correct user account...?"

An attacker with the required customer identifiers could potentially use the flaw to access that customer's account.

From a Suspicious Field to a Proven Bypass

The agent began with reconnaissance, looking at the site's JavaScript and the API calls behind its pages. That analysis surfaced the OTP request and two values that appeared to control how and where the code was sent. Values like those can suggest a hypothesis, but they’re not a finding, since the server might reject the changes or block them later in the login. So the agent built a targeted test around both values and ran it through the live login flow, which confirmed the bypass.

Illustration of the authenticated state the agent reached before stopping. Recreated and anonymized.

Want to see how that testing process works? Book a technical demo to examine how Reflectiz investigates website workflows, validates findings, and controls execution.

Web Context Is the Hard Part

Plenty of automated testing stops at the login gate, but much of what matters sits behind it. A testing system that cannot reach a workflow cannot assess what happens inside it.

Reflectiz solved that problem long before the agent existed. The company has spent more than a decade scanning thousands of production websites, which meant logging in, receiving verification codes, and navigating multi-step flows. So, on sites the company already monitors, the agent starts with that context instead of a blank URL.

Reflectiz's agentic pentesting puts that web context to work. It drives a real browser through the flows a customer follows, including one-time passcodes and 2FA.

Reflectiz CTO and co-founder Ysrael Gurt, a longtime ethical hacker, built the agent on that foundation.

One Finding Is Not a Coverage Report

A confirmed vulnerability may show what failed, but it doesn’t show how much of the application was tested.

Cybersecurity researchers have disclosed details of a new Android banking trojan called Hirudo that works by replacing legitimate banking apps with purpose-built patched versions designed to bypass security checks from inside the app itself, marking a new escalation in financial fraud.

Dutch mobile security company ThreatFabric said it identified replacements for eight Indonesian banking apps, while credential targeting in the malware spans Indonesia, China, India, Mexico, Morocco and Thailand.

"The operation combines credential theft, device takeover, screen and camera capture, and SMS theft, in combination with a fairly mature backend," Eward Driehuis, vice president of fraud engineering at ThreatFabric, said in a statement shared with The Hacker News.

Hirudo facilitates on-device credential theft and live remote control. The malware is delivered by shopping, adult video, and entertainment dropper apps that carry the trojan as a separate installation package, which is then served as an in-app update.

Some of the dropper apps are listed below -

Shopora (com.agbbh.kjdrttt)
1V1 X (com.onev.vip)
KoiShort (com.koishort.app)
ZoyaTV (com.zoyatv.app)

"The lure is functional, loading real content in a WebView, a storefront, a video catalogue or short dramas, so the experience looks legitimate," ThreatFabric explained. "Behind that content the dropper runs a fixed startup routine: it collects promotion-tracking data, fetches its campaign configuration, and checks whether the payload, the Hirudo RAT, is already installed with its accessibility service and notification access enabled."

If it's not present, it displays a fake in-app update prompt to trigger the installation of the malware. It's worth emphasizing that Hirudo is installed as a second app and must be granted its own permissions before it can carry out the malicious activities.

As observed in the case of StreamRat, the malware implements an anti-detection technique based on blocking Internet access by configuring a deliberately non-functional VPN connection prior to the payload installation. This is seen as an attempt to prevent other apps and services, like Google Play Protect, from carrying out cloud-based checks of the payload.

"However, Play Protect also provides offline detection for known potentially harmful applications, meaning that the mechanism does not completely disable its protection," ThreatFabric noted last month. "We therefore assess that the technique is more likely intended to reduce the effectiveness of online reputation and code-analysis mechanisms rather than bypass Play Protect entirely."

Depending on the nature of the lure app used, the dropper is also designed to serve bogus screens to capture payment PINs, serve fake screens requesting login credentials for banks and wallet apps, display fake lock screen pattern and PIN overlays, and facilitate total remote control of the device.

While all this behavior is par for the course when it comes to Android banking trojans, it's their attempts to replace the target banking app with a tampered copy that stand out. Specifically, the purpose-built replacements embed a hooking engine to blind signature, accessibility, screen-capture, and Play Integrity checks from within the app. The replacement targets eight Indonesian apps.

"For these, the RAT detects the installed banking app through accessibility, checks its signing certificate against a stored reference, [and] then shows a fake 'update' prompt," ThreatFabric explained. "It opens Android's uninstaller for the genuine app without waiting for the user to tap, and downloads the bank-specific replacement in […]

Low-cost Android smartphones have been shipped with malicious software baked into the device firmware, allowing bad actors to covertly install apps, conduct ad fraud, and turn devices into residential proxies.

The activity, which targets Android devices built on MediaTek platforms across several brands, is being tracked by Bitdefender under the moniker Midnight Mimosa.

The preinstalled malware ("com.android.system.lite") runs with system-level privileges, which make it possible to install or uninstall a rotating set of at least 32 disguised apps, grant itself additional permissions to accessibility services, notifications, and SMS, and load arbitrary code supplied remotely by the operators.

Specifically, it fetches a remote configuration from an external server and then downloads and executes additional payloads designed to conduct ad fraud and silent installation or removal of partner apps. These apps incorporate proxyware, ad fraud, and code execution features. It can also grant permission to any Android app package.

"This essentially means its operators could install and delete apps at will, tuning each device to their needs, including making them part of large botnets," the Romanian cybersecurity company said.

"This scheme is likely designed mainly to generate revenue. The operators carry out ad and click fraud, collect device and installed-app information, and turn infected devices into residential-proxy relay nodes, making them zombies in botnets."

It's worth emphasizing that the malware itself doesn't engage in fraudulent clicks. Instead, the monetization effort is driven by dropper apps that masquerade as seemingly harmless utility apps, which are responsible for loading genuine ads through a legitimate advertising software development kit (SDK). The end goal is to load an invisible window on top of apps that registers the ads being shown.

In all, Bitdefender said it discovered 13 apps on Google Play that communicate with the same servers that control the malware, indicating the campaign is not limited to preinstalled firmware. Unlike the preinstalled malware, the Play Store apps provide genuine functionality, such as weather information or QR-code scanning. But they also load and display ads outside the apps, including when a user is not actively using the phone.

The names of the apps are listed below. None of them are currently available for download from the Play Store -

Wavrge (com.audify.editor.wavrge)
App Icon DIY (appicon.diy.tools.prop)
Audify (com.audify.editor.pro)
QR Pocket (com.prorestore.qr)
All Deleted Messages Recovery (com.message.recovery.prorestore)
WeatherGo (com.go.weather.mot)
CoolWeather (com.cool.weather.yl)
Daily Weather (com.dmstudio.weather)
Lock & Hide (com.dl.guard.lock)
QuickText Extractor (picturetranslate.extractor.text.lite)
NoteMaster (com.notemaster.record.mark)
Tap to Translate (com.arabmusic.tap.aghani_tamerhosny)
Tasky (org.life.goal.tools)

A notable aspect of the malware is that it disables the Google Play Store app prior to installing a payload app, likely in an attempt to bypass Play Protect safeguards, and then re-enable the app after the payload is run.

What's more, the malware has been detected on devices with firmware signed using certificates attributed to Shenzhen Zediel Co., Ltd, a Chinese Android device manufacturer. However, it's unclear at this stage if the certificate owner was involved in or aware of the malware deployment. However, Bitdefender noted that it also detected other company names over the course of its investigation.

Two of 31 newly disclosed flaws in Progress Software's MarkLogic Server database could let an account given only some management privileges take administrator control of the server, the company says.

Progress published all 31 on October 12 and scored five of them critical. Fixes have been available since September 10, in MarkLogic 11.3.7 and MarkLogic 12.1.0.

Affected releases, and the release that fixes each:

MarkLogic 11.x before 11.3.7: upgrade to 11.3.7
MarkLogic 12.x before 12.1.0: upgrade to 12.1.0

MarkLogic 11.3 is the long-term support (LTS) line. The 12 line, which Progress calls an innovation release, has no patched 12.0 release. Its fix is 12.1.0, which also adds new features.

Installing the fixes for the 10 MarkLogic flaws Progress disclosed in August is not enough. Those fixes arrived in 11.3.6 and 12.0.3, and both releases are affected by the new flaws.

Progress's CVE records and its upgrade notes for the two releases do not say whether any of the 31 flaws has been used in attacks. None was in the U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog when The Hacker News checked on October 13.

The same records and notes list no workaround for customers who cannot upgrade yet.

What the Critical Flaws Allow

Progress scored three of the five critical flaws 9.9 out of 10 on the CVSS scale and the other two 9.6. For each one, the attacker must already have a privilege or a way to run code on the server, according to the company's CVE records.

Two of them involve forests. In MarkLogic, a forest is a collection of documents that is attached to a database.

The fix for CVE-2026-85947 shows which accounts are at issue. A "forest-scoped administrative grant" is no longer enough on its own to attach a forest to a database of the account's choosing, the upgrade notes say. They also tell customers to review delegated forest and database privilege assignments before upgrading, and to audit the roles that hold xdmp-eval-in.

Outside researchers reported four of the five through Bugcrowd. A researcher using the handle rexnets is credited with CVE-2026-85947, CVE-2026-85948, and CVE-2026-85956, and another using the handle WaltWhitehat is credited with CVE-2026-9191.

Flaws That Depend on Configuration

Progress scored 24 of the remaining flaws high and two medium. The highest, CVE-2026-85954, at 8.6, could allow an attacker to gain more privileges than granted by passing values to certain XQuery functions.

Several of the others apply only where a named feature or platform is in use:

Meta is notifying roughly 1,500 people, most of them employees in the US, that their personal information was impacted after hackers got into some of the company’s GitHub repositories.

The intrusion was detected a few weeks ago. According to the tech giant, an outside group gained access to the repositories using an employee’s stolen credentials.

Meta’s security team shut down the attackers’ access and brought in GitHub and law enforcement. Notifications to the impacted individuals started going out on Tuesday.

Meta told SecurityWeek that 99% of the data the hackers took was business data, in the form of software code related to some of its products. The remaining 1% was personal data.

That personal data had been added to the repositories by mistake and should not have been there, as storing it on GitHub went against company policy. Meta has not said what types of personal information were involved.

The company also noted that a significant portion of what looked like personal data was actually synthetic or anonymized test data. As a result, the attackers may not readily be able to tell genuine records apart from test data.

Based on its investigation with GitHub so far, Meta does not believe the hackers were specifically after its data.

Meta is also notifying regulators, and the people whose information was involved are being offered credit and dark web monitoring services.

“This was not a vulnerability in any Meta product, and Meta’s internal systems were not breached. Meta business data held in a GitHub repository was improperly accessed using an employee’s stolen credentials – this included a small amount of personal data for a limited number of people, most of whom were Meta employees,” a Meta spokesperson told SecurityWeek.

In response to the incident, Meta rotated secrets it found in the affected repositories. It also hardened its product security to address risks stemming from access to its business data.

The company is working with its teams that use GitHub to keep user data off the platform. As a second line of defense, it is adding controls for proactive scanning to detect any user data uploaded by mistake.

“We’ve since rotated secrets found in the repositories, implemented new controls to prevent user data from being stored in GitHub, and worked with GitHub on additional measures to protect our repositories,” the spokesperson said.

Adobe has published 11 new security advisories to inform customers about roughly 176 vulnerabilities found and patched in its products.

Adobe Experience Manager (AEM) received patches for 36 vulnerabilities, including several critical flaws allowing arbitrary code execution. The list also includes privilege escalation and security bypass issues.

Adobe ColdFusion updates address 32 vulnerabilities, including critical bugs that can be exploited for code execution and privilege escalation.

A significant number of flaws have been patched by Adobe in the Content Credentials SDK. The product received fixes for 30 vulnerabilities, many described as high-severity issues that can lead to a security feature bypass. Some security holes can be exploited to cause a DoS condition.

Adobe patched 18 vulnerabilities in Photoshop, nearly all allowing arbitrary code execution.

In Substance 3D Stager, Adobe fixed 16 vulnerabilities, including many high-severity arbitrary code execution flaws.

Eleven vulnerabilities have been resolved in Adobe Commerce, including several critical issues that can be exploited without authentication to execute code or escalate privileges.

Several vulnerabilities that allow arbitrary code execution have been fixed in each of the following products: FrameMaker, Dimension, Substance 3D Sampler, Substance 3D Designer, and Bridge.

Adobe says it’s not aware of any in-the-wild exploitation. Most advisories have a priority rating of 3, which indicates Adobe does not expect to see these vulnerabilities exploited in attacks. Commerce and AEM the only products with a priority rating of 2 (threat actors have historically targeted Commerce).

Adobe has been using frontier AI models to hunt for flaws in its own code, which helps explain the higher volume of fixes. However, the company has still credited external researchers for many of the newly patched vulnerabilities.

While AI has helped Adobe find more vulnerabilities in its software, engineers still review, validate, and approve all AI-assisted code changes before deployment.

The rise in discoveries led Adobe to stop publishing security bulletins monthly. The company has moved to a twice-monthly schedule, on the second and fourth Tuesday of each month.
